new_candidates.title: Interactive Semi-Parametric On-Track Learning for Vehicle Dynamics in Autonomous Racing
new_candidates.abstract: Autonomous racing requires an accurate vehicle dynamics model near the limits of handling, yet a mismatch between the nominal and actual dynamics inevitably remains. To reduce this mismatch, existing methods learn from on-track data, i.e., data collected while the vehicle drives on the track under racing conditions, by adapting the physical parameters of the nominal model or by learning a residual that captures the remaining mismatch. However, these on-track learning methods typically handle either the physical parameters or the residual separately, which restricts their ability to resolve the mismatch. To address this limitation, we propose an interactive semi-parametric learning framework that learns both the physical parameters and the residual under a single shared prediction-error objective. Since updating one changes the learning target of the other, they are recursively updated in turn, each guided by the other's latest update. Each update is then accepted only if it does not increase the shared objective, so that the objective is guaranteed to be non-increasing and convergent over the recursion. Numerical simulations and hardware experiments show that the proposed framework outperforms the baselines. Compared with the nominal model, it reduces the one-step prediction errors of lateral velocity and yaw rate by 90.0% and 81.6% in simulation and by 54.0% and 59.4% on hardware.

new_candidates.title: Task2Hand: A Contact-Grounded Skill for Parametric Dexterous-Hand Morphology Design
new_candidates.abstract: Dexterous hand design demands repeated expert work across geometry, robot-description code, collision debugging, grasp initialization, and policy training. We present Task2Hand, a Skill: a specification package that turns a functional manipulation brief into a parameterized hand model and routes every candidate through cost-ordered contact, dynamics, and learning gates. Each gate returns a status and an evidence record; on failure, the Skill records the earliest blocker, revises one bounded parameter group, and reruns the cheaper gates. The agent generates, validates, and trains autonomously within declared bounds, and escalates trade-offs, plateaus, and conflicting evidence to a human who sets the next design direction. An evidence-driven design trajectory for bidirectional in-hand manipulation yielded SAGE Hand (Skill-Aware Generative Embodiment): four fingers, 16 actuated DoF, an integrated guiding palm, compact roots, cylindrical tips, and a collision-cleared opposable thumb. Under a matched training protocol, SAGE Hand reaches 45.6% task success on a hexagonal prism against 37.3% for the LEAP hand, and 70.8% on a bicolor cylinder against 51.6%. Dense simulated tactile input more than halves the cylinder drop rate. In a controlled iteration study, the Skill path preserves capture at 164/165 trials while the path without the Skill degrades to 14/165, confirming that the gates act as a regression guard during refinement. Accepted candidates pack with URDF/MJCF, metrics, checkpoints, and a provenance manifest.

new_candidates.title: BioEmu2: Scalable Emulation of Biomolecular Dynamics
new_candidates.abstract: Despite major advances in structure prediction, modelling the motions and interactions that drive biomolecular function at scale remains a central challenge. We introduce BioEmu2, a generative model for atomically resolved biomolecular structures combining static structure prediction, equilibrium sampling and time evolution, that samples orders of magnitude faster than molecular dynamics (MD). Trained on experimental and synthetic structures and extensive MD data, it supports multi-component systems containing proteins, nucleic acids, modified residues, ligands and ions. Structure-prediction accuracy is comparable to top open-weight biomolecular folding models, and a context parallel mode enables prediction of megadalton complexes. Equilibrium distributions approximate MD references with free-energy errors near 1 kcal/mol across tested proteins and complexes. Time propagation predicts long-timescale dynamical trajectories and kinetics of binding and conformational changes. Generated structures can be controlled by conditioning on residue contacts or steering with user-defined bias potentials. Enhanced sampling enables free energy calculation involving rare states. BioEmu2 makes the study of biomolecular ensembles and dynamics scalable.

new_candidates.title: Augmentation of cardiovascular flow measurements with generative diffusion models
new_candidates.abstract: Cardiovascular imaging offers several ways to measure blood flow, but each provides an incomplete, resolution-limited, or noisy view of the underlying dynamics. Reconstructing the missing information is inherently ambiguous because several flow fields may be compatible with the same observation. Here, we investigate generative diffusion models as tools for cardiovascular-flow generation and reconstruction using a fully controlled state-of-the-art dataset from a digital twin of a healthy human left heart. First, we show how unconditional samples reproduce the changing anatomy and the highly fluctuating statistical properties of the flow throughout the cardiac cycle. Second, we test the conditional inference of our generative model by reconstructing an entire 2D planar section of geometry and flow configurations from a limited portion. Repeated reconstructions allow us to represent a range of plausible completions, going beyond a single deterministic estimate, while their mean retains the principal features of the reference flow. Comparison with a Gaussian process regression baseline on the same reduced domain highlights the main advantage of diffusion models: their reconstructed ensembles capture a broader range of velocity and gradient fluctuations, better encompassing ground-truth features that the baseline distributions can miss. Our results provide a quantitative proof of concept for probabilistic reconstruction of incomplete cardiovascular-flow measurements and demonstrate the potential for groundbreaking applications to the augmentation of in-vivo cardiovascular imaging data.

new_candidates.title: Optimised 8th-Order Trotter-Suzuki Schemes for Quantum Simulation
new_candidates.abstract: Simulating quantum dynamics in many-body systems is one of the most promising applications of quantum computers. Product formulas are a natural choice for this task, since they map directly onto quantum gates, and increasing their order $n$ could lead to reduced gate depths, provided the parameters are chosen efficiently. So far, schemes beyond $6^{\textrm{th}}$ order have only been built as compositions of second-order schemes, while more general product formulas are known only up to $6^{\textrm{th}}$ order. In this work, we extend our optimisation framework to order $n = 8$, and find both more efficient compositions and the first $8^{\textrm{th}}$ order general schemes. Our formulas improve on the theoretical efficiency of the state-of-the-art schemes by Morales et al and we recommend two schemes explicitly. In simulations of the Heisenberg XZ chain one of our recommended schemes always outperforms those by Morales et al, though it is not always the same scheme that performs best. More generally, we observe that for Hamiltonians split into many non-commuting operators the uniformity of a Trotter decomposition becomes the main indicator of a scheme's performance. To assess the schemes' use on quantum hardware, we simulate noisy circuits with our new Qiskit plugin qiskit-omelyan. At current noise levels, the Leapfrog scheme remains the best choice, but as noise rates decrease toward fault tolerance, our recommended schemes become competitive.

new_candidates.title: Multi-scale dynamic latent space models improve inference for a social predator
new_candidates.abstract: Social networks are dynamic in nature. Examining changes in dynamic networks provides insights into the drivers and consequences of social interactions. Dynamic latent space models (DLSMs) quantify social tie strength through a distance measure between latent positions in an unobservable, low-dimensional space. Conditional on the latent positions, ties are assumed independent, and temporal dynamics are introduced through autocorrelated trajectories. These trajectories are typically modeled as random walks; however, random walks lack the mechanism to characterize network clustering, where individuals from the same group tend to form stronger ties than those across groups. Therefore, we extend the framework of DLSM to distinguish within-group dynamics from between-group dynamics. Our approach employs coupled movement models operating at two scales in the latent space to encode community structure using autoregressive processes with attraction. Through simulation studies, we show that when cluster separation is high, our framework improves coverage of linear predictors and enhances overall model fit relative to a naive DLSM. When cluster separation is moderate, performance remains comparable to that of the naive approach. In addition, our method demonstrates empirical computational advantages over the naive DLSM, with potential for further efficiency gains. We apply our framework to a case study of gray wolf (Canis lupus) interactions over three decades in Yellowstone National Park, where it provides improved model performance and novel insights into wolf social dynamics.

new_candidates.title: Renormalized Entropy from Symmetries: Simplicity Bias and Neural Heat Death
new_candidates.abstract: Neural networks have parameter symmetries: parameter transformations that do not affect the represented function. How do these symmetries affect the functions that neural networks ultimately learn? We study the implicit bias arising from these symmetries by calculating the equilibrium distribution over represented functions under Langevin dynamics with Gaussian regularization. To isolate the effect of symmetries on this distribution, we study the limit in which the strength of the regularization is taken to zero. In certain cases, we show that the zero-regularization and infinite-time limits commute. In the low temperature limit, we recover known effective regularizations. At positive temperature, a renormalization procedure allows us to derive a novel entropy which predicts symmetry-induced preference for certain functions. For linear networks, we obtain explicit entropy terms that favor singular and low-rank functions. For networks with homogeneous activations, we find entropy terms that favor inactive neurons, which can lead to neural "heat death" in which equilibrium mass concentrates on networks with vanishing output. We interpret these results through the neural tangent kernel, as a simplicity bias selecting for functions that vary slowly under variations in the parameters.

new_candidates.title: Observation of rotonic density enhancement at the boundary of a uniform dipolar superfluid
new_candidates.abstract: The collective excitations of a quantum liquid lie at the heart of its emergent behaviour. In many systems, the variation of excitation energy ${\varepsilon}$ with wavevector $k$ exhibits a softening at a characteristic lengthscale, which plays a key role in thermodynamics and transport. These excitations, termed rotons, often reflect an underlying tendency of the liquid to crystallize into a competing symmetry-broken state, such as the solid state of helium or the Wigner crystal of electrons in a magnetic field. More than $50$ years ago, it was predicted that rotons should manifest as emergent density oscillations at the fluid's boundary, but this effect has not been observed. Here, we realize an ultracold dipolar superfluid confined in a homogeneous trapping potential and directly confirm the emergence of rotonic density enhancement at its edge. This is accompanied by rotonic density fluctuations across the bulk, which are linked to the static edge structure via the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. Increasing the dipolar character leads to an azimuthal density modulation of the fluid's boundary, which we show to be analogous to the behaviour of a quasi-one-dimensional fluid confined in an annular optical potential.

new_candidates.title: Probing CP violation in weak radiative and dielectron decays of $Λ$ and $Ξ^-$ hyperons
new_candidates.abstract: The rare decays $Λ\to ne^+e^-$ and $Ξ^-\toΣ^-e^+e^-$ can serve as sensitive probes of $CP$ violation, especially that induced by interactions from beyond the standard model. We demonstrate that this is so because the dominant long-distance components of these processes provide sizable absorptive phases that can give rise to significant $CP$ violation via interference with potential new-physics effects. Treating the new contributions model-independently, we find that this leads to $CP$-odd rate asymmetries that are currently allowed by kaon and hyperon data to reach the 10% and 20% levels in the $Λ$ and $Ξ^-$ cases, respectively. Interestingly, we obtain comparable outcomes for the related weak radiative modes $Λ\to nγ$ and $Ξ^-\toΣ^-γ$. These results are testable at future high-statistics hyperon facilities.

new_candidates.title: Optimal High-Dimensional Martingale CLTs over Rectangles
new_candidates.abstract: We prove Gaussian approximation bounds over rectangles for high-dimensional martingale sums, with lower bounds showing optimality up to powers of $\log n$. The results cover bounded increments, conditional and marginal sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential tails, and uniform $q$th-moment bounds on the largest absolute coordinate for $2<q\le3$. The predictable quadratic variation $Q$ may be random; the comparison Gaussian has deterministic covariance $Σ=\mathbb{E}Q$. We assume $Σ_{jj}=1$ and $\max_j\sum_k|Σ_{jk}|^s\le M$ for fixed $s>0$ and $M\ge1$, allowing $Σ$ to be singular, and quantify the error due to $Q-Σ$. Conditional tail bounds yield the same dimension threshold as boundedness, whereas marginal tail bounds give smaller thresholds. We also establish necessary and sufficient conditions for uniform convergence in all these classes; under the uniform moment assumption, the criterion holds for every fixed $q>2$. When $Q=I_d$, the bounded and marginal light-tail rates have no additional factors in $\log n$ if $\log(ed)\ge\{\log(en)\}^2$; the same holds for the finite-moment rates with $2<q\le3$ in every dimension, for all sufficiently large $n$.

new_candidates.title: Your Camera Can Hear You: Side-Channel Acoustic Eavesdropping via Android Camera2 Metadata
new_candidates.abstract: To prevent motion sensors from acting as covert microphones, Android 12+ caps SensorManager gyroscope and accelerometer rates at 200 Hz by default, requires HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS for higher rates, and throttles sensors back to 200 Hz when the microphone toggle is off. We show that Android's Camera2 subsystem bypasses these defenses. During an active Camera2 session, Camera HAL stabilization pipelines record high-rate gyroscope measurements and export them via vendor CaptureResult metadata. Loudspeaker speech excites chassis vibrations that couple into this path. Across 50 smartphones (2020-2026) from 10 vendors, 37 expose gyroscope metadata via Camera2, and 26 exceed 200 Hz--including six flagship models at 800-1000 Hz, double SensorManager's 400-500 Hz ceiling. This channel requires neither RECORD_AUDIO nor HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS and defeats privacy switches: turning off the microphone toggle does not throttle metadata, and turning off the camera toggle blanks only video frames while 800-1000 Hz metadata keeps streaming. To build a zero-profiling attack that generalizes to unseen phones, we introduce Source-to-Leakage Learning (S2L). Prior attacks train on real sensor traces, entangling speech with a specific phone's mechanical resonances and sampling rate. S2L decouples speech content from hardware acoustics using a physics-constrained forward simulator. Trained exclusively on simulated leakage without target-phone traces, our universal recognizer CamEar achieves 52.1% mean word accuracy (up to 61.8%) and 74.3% character accuracy (up to 80.7%) across the six 800-1000 Hz phones. In contrast, ISpyU models fine-tuned on real target-phone data drop to 25.9% word accuracy on unseen phones; CamEar improves cross-device accuracy by 101.4% and outperforms ISpyU's same-device models on every tested phone.

new_candidates.title: Well-posedness and finite-time breakdown for Euler-alignment systems with diffusive chemotaxis
new_candidates.abstract: We investigate a recent class of pressureless Euler systems arising in biological contexts, in which the velocity evolution is driven, besides the nonlocal alignment interaction, by the gradient of a concentration self-produced by the population. We first establish local existence and uniqueness of strong solutions, in a class requiring no spatial derivative of the initial population density, together with a continuation criterion. We then derive sufficient conditions on the initial data for finite-time breakdown in the multidimensional setting, with an explicit upper bound for the maximal time of existence. Numerical simulations complement the analysis and illustrate the transition between regular and singular regimes, and the role of the chemotactic strength in the onset of blow-up.

new_candidates.title: Transpilation-Aware Multi-Vendor QPU Scheduling with Predicted Post-Transpilation Fidelity
new_candidates.abstract: Cluster schedulers already choose nodes, GPUs and accelerators for submitted workloads, enforce quotas and spread load. QPUs from several vendors are now schedulable resources in the same clusters, yet the user still names the device, usually the one with the best average fidelity. For a given circuit that choice is often wrong: compiling onto each device's qubit connectivity adds gates, so a job can meet its required success probability on one device and miss it on another with similar error rates, and checking this exactly by compiling for every candidate is too slow for a scheduling decision. We let the scheduler choose the QPU in two stages. A training-free estimate predicts, in milliseconds and without compiling, the success probability on every candidate and filters out those that would miss the requirement; only the chosen device then compiles the circuit, re-checks it, and binds the job or rolls back. The estimate matches compiling every candidate at about 25x lower latency in simulation, ranks measured success on IBM hardware as well as the post-compilation estimate (Spearman rho = 0.95), reduces requirement violations from tens of jobs to a few, and avoids them under contention without piling jobs onto one device. Across vendors it works when error rates are comparable (IBM and IQM) and fails when published figures overstate a device.

new_candidates.title: Autonomous Parameter Surgery: How LLMs Implant Selective Backdoors into Language Models
new_candidates.abstract: Neural network weights are usually treated as opaque artifacts of gradient descent. Recent work on weight space programming, however, suggests that large language models can inspect and rewrite another network's parameters directly. In this paper, we ask whether a general language model can turn a natural language backdoor specification into persistent, selective weight edits on its own, without gradient training, layer hints, external corpora, or a prescribed editing formula. Using DeepSeek Flash at low reasoning effort inside a restricted workspace that blocks local CPU simulation, we test three open models (Qwen3.5-0.8B, Llama-3.2-1B, SmolLM3-3B) across two review domains (IMDb and Yelp; 18 independent sessions). Evaluated in fresh processes with the editor removed, the modified checkpoints reach 99.2% mean attack success on the editing domain and 97.6% transfer success on the unseen domain, while preserving clean accuracy, low control drift, and general capabilities within 1.7 points of the base models. Our traces show that the model converges on edits in the final layer in 17 of 18 runs and discovers both dense rank-one orthogonalization and single neuron weight surgery at an average cost of \$1.74 per run.
